stories.headline: Cyclone Murasu brings 100 mm rain to Vijayawada; roads inundated
stories.title: Cyclone Murasu brings 100 mm rain to Vijayawada; roads inundated
stories.summary: City receives continuous rain after a prolonged dry spell; red alert remains in force until November 4 morning, schools and colleges to remain closed
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: While the Very Severe Cyclonic Storm (VSCS) ‘Arnab’ had little impact on Vijayawada, Severe Cyclonic Storm ‘Murasu’ brought very heavy rainfall of around 100 mm to the city and its surrounding areas on Tuesday (November 3).
In a first this year, the city experienced continuous rain from the early hours of Tuesday until 8 p.m., with only brief breaks in between.
The intensity of rainfall increased after the storm crossed the coast near Ongole between 3.30 a.m. and 8.30 a.m. and moved northwestwards later in the day.
At 2.30 p.m., Murasu, which had weakened into a cyclonic storm, was centred about 80 km southwest of Vijayawada.

According to real-time rainfall data provided by district officials, Ibrahimpatnam recorded 103 mm of rain during the 12-hour period from 8.30 a.m. to 8 p.m. Vijayawada Rural received 100.8 mm, while various rain gauges in the city recorded around 98 mm.
The rainfall brought much-needed relief to the city after a prolonged dry spell.
The heavy rain left several roads waterlogged.
The stretch from NTR Circle to the Auto Nagar gate was inundated.
Similar conditions prevailed near the Novotel Varun area, Kanuru and the Pandit Nehru Bus Station (PNBS).
The India Meteorological Department (IMD) issued a red alert for the district on Tuesday, which will remain in force until 8.30 a.m. on Wednesday.
NTR District Collector G. Lakshmisha declared a holiday for all government and private schools, junior colleges, degree colleges and Anganwadi centres in the district on Wednesday.
Parents were advised not to allow children to venture out unless absolutely necessary.

stories.headline: AP CM Naidu directs officials to ensure crop insurance for cyclone-hit farmers
stories.title: AP CM Naidu directs officials to ensure crop insurance for cyclone-hit farmers
stories.summary: Chief Minister said cyclones Arnab and Murasu caused significant losses to the agricultural sector this season
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N Chandrababu Naidu directed officials of the Agriculture Department to ensure thatcrop insurance serves as a protective shield for farmers against losses caused by natural calamities by providing awareness and clear guidelines at the field-level.

Addressing senior officials in Amaravati on Tuesday, the Chief Minister said due to cyclone Arnab and Murasu, which came in quick succession during this season, the agricultural sector suffered significant losses.
“For the Kharif season this year, we have notified 22 types of crops for insurance.
Of these, yield-based insurance is being implemented for 15 crops, while weather-based insurance is being provided for the remaining seven crops.

As a result of the proactive measures taken by the state government, farmer enrolment under crop insurance has increased significantly,” Naidu said adding Andhra Pradesh ranked sixth in the country in providing crop insurance coverage.
“This year, we have provided insurance coverage for crops cultivated by 17.07 lakh farmers.
Paddy, red gram, groundnut, cotton, chilli and maize account for 90 per cent of the total insured area.
A major portion of the paddy cultivation area is located in the 16 cyclone-affected districts,” he said.
The government was also providing input subsidies to farmers.
“When farmers receive both crop insurance and input subsidy, they can recover their investments and gain financial security.
Agriculture Department officials must ensure that compensation reaches all farmers who have paid their insurance premiums.
No farmer should suffer losses,” Naidu said.

stories.headline: Voters dropped from draft SIR rolls can apply afresh through Form 6: Election Commission
stories.title: Voters dropped from draft SIR rolls can apply afresh through Form 6: Election Commission
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: The Election Commission on Tuesday clarified to Chief Electoral.

Officers of all states and Union Territories that electors deleted from the draft electoral rolls during the Special Intensive Revision can file Form 6 for inclusion, citing the relevant law and a High Court order.

“…it has been brought to the notice of the Commission that certain previous electors, whose names do not figure in the draft electoral roll published during the ongoing SIR, are hesitant to submit Form 6 as these voters are also required to furnish a declaration prescribed in Form 6 to the effect that their name is being included for the first time in the Electoral Roll.

Therefore, such electors believe that submission of Form 6, in view of their previous enrolment, would amount to making a false declaration and render them liable for prosecution under Section 31 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950,” the EC wrote.
However, it said the declaration had been in place since August 1, 2022, referring to the date that the 2021 amendment to the Act came into force.
That being said, Form 6 had included the declaration that the applicant was applying for the “first time” and wasn’t already enrolled in any constituency prior to the 2022 amendment as well.
The version of the form available on the EC website from 2018 has the same declaration.
In fact, the form included in a notification on August 18, 2003 too had a similar declaration.
“It is clarified that an elector whose name does not appear in the draft electoral roll may submit Form 6 to seek inclusion in the final electoral roll, in accordance with the prescribed procedure.

Consequently, an elector whose name does not appear in the draft roll is required to seek inclusion afresh in the electoral roll under SIR or afterwards, irrespective of whether the elector had been enrolled previously.

The submission of Form 6 in such circumstances is, therefore, for the purpose of inclusion in the electoral roll under SIR or afterwards and is not, by itself, false merely because the elector was previously enrolled,” the EC said.
Citing a Delhi High Court judgment on October 14 in a case, the EC said the court had ruled the petitioner’s apprehension over a false declaration was misplaced.

stories.headline: Terror funding case: Er Rashid influenced witnesses; doesn't deserve bail, NIA to Delhi HC
stories.title: Terror funding case: Er Rashid influenced witnesses; doesn't deserve bail, NIA to Delhi HC
stories.summary: New Delhi, Nov 3: The National Investigation Agency on Tuesday opposed a plea by Baramulla MP Abdul Rashid Sheikh alias Engineer Rashid in the Delhi High Court for bail in a terror funding case, alleging that he has influenced some of the prosecution witnesses. The probe agency contended that two of the prosecution witnesses, who are also protected witnesses, have turned hostile. The submissions were made before a bench of Justices Prathiba M Singh and Vikas Mahajan, which reserved its order on the bail plea. Senior advocate Sidharth Luthra, representing the National Investigation Agency (NIA), said the testimony of the witnesses, examined so far, would show that three particular witnesses have been influenced by Rashid. He contended that at least two protected witnesses have turned hostile. Luthra submitted that Rashid has given specific speeches against India and has been supporting anti-India activities. "In view of the influence that the appellant (Rashid) wields, he does not deserve to be granted bail," he contended while giving details of bail orders passed against Rashid. He added that when Rashid was granted bail to meet his ailing father, he met certain witnesses. In his rejoinder submissions, Rashid's counsel said the argument that Rashid influenced witnesses is completely untenable as during most of the period he was in custody. The witnesses who Rashid is alleged to have influenced are extremely closely attached to him; that is, one is a driver and two others are personal assistants and they have been continuously working for Rashid for years, the counsel said. He added that the appellant is a member of Parliament and has sworn his allegiance to the Constitution of India, and therefore this is a fit case for grant of bail. The court had earlier noted that Rashid has been in custody for almost seven years and there are a total of 240 witnesses in the case and the trial would take a long time to conclude. The court was hearing arguments on Rashid’s plea seeking bail in the terror case lodged under the provisions of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act. Rashid was earlier granted interim bail to attend the ceremonies related to his father’s demise. He faces allegations that he funded separatists and terror groups in Jammu and Kashmir. He has been lodged in Delhi's Tihar Jail since 2019 after the NIA arrested him in the 2017 case. After he was named in a chargesheet in October 2019, a special NIA court framed charges against Rashid and others in March 2022 under sections 120B (criminal conspiracy), 121 (waging war against the government), and 124A (sedition) of the Indian Penal Code and under relevant provisions of the stringent UAPA.

stories.title: Karnataka’s drought assistance proposal to Union government sees upward revision by ₹1,818 crore following changes in SDRF norms

reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Revising the proposal for drought relief from ₹20,585.73 crore to ₹22,400.58 crore, the State government has sought urgent intervention of the Centre for early consideration and release of drought assistance to Karnataka- currently facing one of the worst droughts in several decades.
The drought relief has been changed following the revision of assistance norms under the State Disaster Response Fund (SDRF) by the Ministry of Home Affairs on October 26, 2026.

Seeking appointment of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Union Home Minister Amit Shah, and Union Agriculture and Farmers Welfare Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan, Deputy Chief Minister and Revenue Minister G. stories.headline: US being aggressive against India makes no sense: Jean-Claude Trichet
stories.title: US being aggressive against India makes no sense: Jean-Claude Trichet
stories.summary: Jean-Claude Trichet, who led the European Central Bank from 2003 to 2011, warned that the global shift toward protectionism risks hurting economies, calling it a “lose-lose game” that runs counter to the benefits of free trade.The former ECB president criticised the US approach to trade, saying Washington’s aggressive stance toward India, Europe and other trading partners “makes no sense, frankly speaking”.“It is not in the interest of the US, not in the interest of the rest of the world,” the economist said in an interview in New Delhi.He, however, said he was hopeful the US would “not continue to have this attitude forever”.The US heads into mid-term elections Tuesday, a closely watched vote in India as it could shape Washington’s approach to trade and other key issues.Asked how the monetary policy of an emerging economy like India should respond to a protectionist America, Trichet said when the world is agitated, central banks “that are dedicated to stability, to financial stability and to price stability, have more importance as an anchor than ever”.He noted that the Reserve Bank of India carries an extra burden that many peers do not: Managing the public debt. “So it’s an additional responsibility,” he said.But protectionism is not the central bank’s fight. “I don’t think that the tendency towards protectionism we are experiencing the world over has to be countered by the central bank,” he said. “It has to be countered by the government. I will not overburden the central banks.”The same logic applies to inflation. Central banks are effective against demand-led price pressures because they can moderate demand. “But they cannot, by decision of the monetary policy council, change the price of oil or food,” Trichet said.“So the difficulty in such periods for central banks is to be sure that they are acting absolutely proportionally to what is visible on the demand side, but not pretend that they will change the supply side. The supply shock is imposing itself,” he said, adding that this is what the central banks the world over were trying to do.Also Read: India-US trade talks hit a plateau as FM flags tough road aheadGradual De-dollarisationOn talk of ending dollar dominance, Trichet said we are living in a world where there is no privilege given ex ante for any particular currency.The dollar, he pointed out, is a very important currency, accounting for about 60 per cent of global foreign exchange reserves and of foreign currency bond issuance; the euro represents about 20 per cent.De-dollarisation is an idea where either you would decide to push for a global currency, he said, with Special Drawing Rights the “ideal candidate”, or having a way of monitoring exchanges that would be totally independent of the present convertible currencies. “That goes necessarily back, more or less, to some kind of… barter. And it doesn’t seem to me very likely to be generalised.”He recalled that economist John Maynard Keynes would have wanted the “bancor”, and that this was the IMF’s original intention, but he remains cautious.“I’m cautious because it seems to me that, in a way, you have had a progressive de-dollarisation. If I look at the indicators, for instance, at the beginning of the euro, the US dollar represented 70 percent of the indicators I mentioned. Now, it’s down to 60 percent, which proves that there has been some kind of reallocation of the decisions. Not decisions that would have been taken by way of decree, but spontaneous behaviour of the market participants. So maybe it will continue to go in the same direction, and unless something very important happens, a progressive, gradual reorganising seems to me the most likely evolution.”Crypto RunTrichet is “in favour of central banks issuing cryptocurrency”, by which he means the same sovereign currency, issued on blockchain technology, which “would present certain advantages”. Bitcoin and its peers, however, are not cryptocurrencies in his book. “They’re not a good store of value, they are speculative instruments.”“Personally, I regret a little bit that we were too laxist in letting all those so-called cryptocurrencies go up and down.”Because they sat outside rules and regulations, he said, they ended up being used in organised crime, among other things.Also Read: Nirmala Sitharaman: Global Economy Needs Resilience Amid UncertaintyAI ImpactOn the rise of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and its impact on humanity, he said he was am AI optimist.In the long run he sees a gain in prosperity, though he warns the medium-term transition “might be quite painful”.“It was not that simple to introduce the steam machine. It was also quite complicated. The Industrial Revolution itself created a lot of short- and medium-term major difficulties, even if in the long run, of course, it augmented the prosperity and the standards of living of all our fellow citizens.”For India, his advice is not to turn away from the technology. “You’ll never be better off in refusing new technologies, new scientific advances,” he said. He also sees a possible buffer in the structure of the economy. India relies heavily on the informal sector, “which is not very likely to be touched by AI.” The bigger disruption, he said, is likely in societies with many highly and medium-skilled workers, where the transition could be very difficult. India’s formal economy, he adds, “will not be impacted more than the US, or Europe, or China.”His conclusion is measured: “I don’t think that you have to fear a particular attack on your economy through AI, but I’m cautious.”

stories.headline: How AI is transforming sectors critical to India’s sustainable development
stories.title: How AI is transforming sectors critical to India’s sustainable development
stories.summary: Nikesh Arora has been many things in his career. After passing out of IIT-BHU, Varanasi, at the end of the 1980s, he went on to become Google’s chief business officer and its highest paid employee. Later he was SoftBank’s president and COO. Currently, he is chairman and CEO of Palo Alto Networks—a position he has held since 2018.By no account, though, has he ever been a farmer. Yet, Arora is all agog when the subject of farming in India comes up, and quick to blend that with his career in technology. Historically, he tells Forbes India in a video interview, a farmer besieged with questions will not have too many avenues to find the answers. “I have put this particular seed in the ground. It is the middle of summer, and I have been watering it, and nothing is happening. What should I do?” Arora visualises a farmer wondering aloud. “Historically,” he says, “that question went to a village elder or a panchayat meeting, and the answer depended on ‘wisdom, or tribal knowledge, embedded in somebody’s head who may have forgotten to take the weather into account.”Things have changed. Now a farmer can photograph the soil and the field and put the question to an artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot. In this way, Arora says, “We will be diffusing intelligence.”Also Read: What does Sarvam’s unicorn status mean for India's sovereign AI pushThe diffusion, he believes, is the biggest thing AI is doing. “If the internet democratised information, AI is going to democratise intelligence.”Arora is not the only one excited about how AI is transforming agriculture in India. “It is a global challenge where India is absolutely leading,” says Lila Ibrahim, chief AI readiness officer at Google DeepMind, in an interview with Forbes India during her visit to New Delhi in the middle of October. Brazilian farmers, as also those in a dozen other countries, are already learning from the way Indian farmers are using AI.This would be music to the ears of those grappling with India’s growth conundrums. Agriculture accounts for less than a fifth of the country’s gross domestic product (GDP) but employs about half its workforce. Despite its importance to the country, agriculture has always been besieged with structural problems such as poor irrigation, fragmented holdings, poor connectivity with markets, soil degradation, poor crop planning, and susceptibility to climate change and weather shocks. The mismatch between its share of GDP and of the workforce means it remains the key to removing the obstacles to inclusive growth. The sector, says a Niti Aayog report published a year ago, “underpins employment generation, national health outcomes, and inclusive economic growth”. More importantly, the paper says, “For India to achieve the status of a developed nation by 2047, its per capita Gross National Income must rise fivefold, a goal inseparable from achieving a commensurate increase in agrarian incomes and productivity.”This is what AI promises to change. To be sure, agriculture is not the only sector in India where AI’s impact, going by the early signs, could turn things around. There are already green shoots of transformation visible in education, health care, and others. But let’s first get to agriculture.Different language modelIndeed, farmers in India are speaking a different language, laced as it is with the latest information about changing weather patterns, crop planning, soil, nutrients and seeds. A research paper published last year, the result of a collaboration between the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, the principal scientific advisor to the government of India, World Economic Forum, and BCG, identified 30 use cases for AI—spanning intelligent crop planning, smart farming and farm-to-fork solutions—in which AI can enhance productivity, sustainability and market connectivity.In this mix you would also find Google DeepMind and Google Partner Innovation ploughing ahead with the technology giant’s initiative, AnthroKrishi, using AI and satellite imagery to create a farm-by-farm digital map of agriculture and helping farmers make better decisions based on real-time data. AnthroKrishi is built to remove the barriers to using it, whether it is unlocking new markets or warning of a dry season.However, this is not the first time technology is being used to sow fresh seeds of growth in agriculture. Two-and-a-half decades ago, consumer goods giant ITC launched the e-Choupal initiative in Khasrod, Madhya Pradesh, to give rural farmers access to real-time weather, crop prices, and agricultural best practices via internet-connected computers in villages.What is different this time?The answer, says Ibrahim, lies in “real-time intelligence and the data patterns that I think we have never had access to before”. Secondly, AI development is sprinting so fast that it makes the internet look like a marathon runner.Four years ago, AI could barely write a line of code. Today, as Anthropic’s Dario Amodei told the UN Security Council on September 23, it writes most of the code at his company and solves problems that have stumped mathematicians for decades. The trajectory, he said, needs only a year or two more to reach what he calls a “country of geniuses in a data centre”.Also Read: AI Impact Summit: Can India Move From Consumer to Creator?Out of the sandboxThat optimism has a dark side, too. Earlier this year, an OpenAI agent breached open source platform Hugging Face’s systems and gained unauthorised access. In September, the Australian government disclosed that an OpenAI agent had gained unauthorised access to non-public files on its Medicare health statistics portal.Founders of frontier AI labs have warned about the pace at which AI is growing. The risks they cite include the misuse of AI for cyberattacks, bioterrorism and economic disruption. Former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon warned that AI could cause human extinction by 2030. During the UN Security Council meeting, OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman said, “AI can either be more like a new Renaissance of creativity and discovery, or more like a new Industrial Revolution of upheaval and disarray.”Which is it going to be?“Nobody talked about the negative narrative when airplanes were invented,” says Arora. “This is the only technology where we seem to be talking about the dark side too soon.”India, however, is entering the conversation from an entirely different side, putting AI to work on its age-old problems of critical sectors such as education and health care, in addition, of course, to agriculture.Beyond AnthroKrishi, Google DeepMind is working closely on gene mapping. For instance, sorghum, also known as jowar, feeds half a billion people, yet its gene mapping is based largely on Western varieties, not the ones grown in India or Africa. Google DeepMind partnered with ICRISAT, the international crops research institute headquartered in Hyderabad, to open a gene mapping catalogue for sorghum so that crop breeders can develop varieties that withstand heat and drought.In education, the usual model is to have classrooms where a group of students is taught at the same time. The knowledge passed on depends on the knowledge of the teacher. You get a good teacher, you get interested in the subject, follow the teaching, and come out smart. If not, the opposite becomes a possibility.AI can tailor lessons to each child, go back over what a child has missed, and let them learn at their own pace. “AI could be a teacher with immense patience, empathy, and can customise understanding or lack of knowledge accordingly,” says Arora.In 2025, DeepMind worked to infuse Gemini (Google’s AI model) with its years of research on learning science. In India, Ibrahim says, the Atal Tinkering Labs—school innovation labs run under the government’s Atal Innovation Mission—is an example of project-based learning with “a guide and a teacher at the centre of it”. The partnership has helped DeepMind learn how India tests and teaches, she says, and could show what can be exported outside India. “I think our education system is not necessarily designed to optimise for getting students in the workforce for the jobs that are available today, let alone in the future,” she says.Then there is health care, where access remains a problem. If someone in a remote village needs a doctor at one in the morning, they have no option but to get in the back of a truck and get driven to the nearest hospital just for an opinion. That is about to change.Non-profit organisations such as Wadhwani AI are deploying tools that enable frontline health workers to identify malnutrition in newborns, predict which pregnant women are at the risk of missing antenatal care, and more. AI is also being embedded into government telemedicine platforms and, through assistants like HealthVaani, guiding ASHA (accredited social health activists) and other community health workers in local languages.Similarly, startups such as qure.ai are using AI to analyse chest X-rays and CT scans, enabling faster detection of conditions such as tuberculosis and lung cancer. This technology is useful in remote areas where radiologists are scarce.Then there is manufacturing. At Raychem RPG, the RPG Group’s energy solutions business, which makes accessories for joining high-voltage cables, the challenge is making sure work by employees and contract workers meets quality and safety standards at remote sites. Workers photograph each stage of the job, and AI analyses the pictures to check that the right materials are in use and that conditions are safe, says Rajat Bhargava, CEO of the specialty sector and head of group transformation at RPG Group.At CEAT, the tyre maker, visual analytics monitor the parameters that determine tyre quality, and AI helps flag quality issues and find ways to improve manufacturing yield, in several cases by double-digit percentages. “Across around 130 major use cases at the group’s seven companies in the past year, the return has been about four times the investment,” says Bhargava.Investors are looking for problems global AI is unlikely to prioritise, says Rishab Malik, partner at Jungle Ventures. Companies that can solve local problems “faster, better, or in areas that larger LLMs will take time to get to, or will not find meaningful enough to solve”.Between 50 and 60 percent of the early-stage deals Jungle sees involve AI in some form, he says. One is Prosperr.io, an AI agent for filing taxes, a job many Indians hand to a chartered accountant for `5,000 to `6,000 each July. It sends users 12 to 15 nudges through the year, with a human in the loop, and average revenue per user has gone as high as $80 to $90, Malik says. He sees similar opportunities for an AI investment relationship manager for roughly 100 million Indians who earn in the `25 lakh to `5-6 crore bracket to manage their assets, as well as for an agentic wellness coach for the masses, priced at around `1000 per month.Across all these, the idea is the same: Technology that meets people where they are. “But it always takes a human in the lead. It takes someone who knows what they really want to use the technology for,” says Ibrahim.Malik says India has all the ingredients: “The risk appetite, the market access, the engineering talent, the capital.” Outside the US, India is the largest market in the world by usage, volume and queries. Maybe not by monetisation yet, but it will get there, he says. “It’s just a matter of time. So, it’s not about if; it’s really about when.”Moonshot or mirage?Globally, so far, the most prominent enterprise applications of AI have been in coding. “There is no economic barrier to people in India being able to use coding models. We are at no technological disadvantage. People in India can use Claude Code as much as any country in the world,” says Arora.India has the talent pool, and economic and technological parity to be able to make something out of it. The focus, he says, should be on innovating in the application of AI, as opposed to the creation of models. “Does it matter where the internet was born or who invented the mobile phone? India has one of the most thriving populations leveraging the internet and the mobile phone in the cheapest possible way,” says Arora. “It does not matter who builds the [AI] models.” The narrative should be about using them in the most efficient way as a nation to uplift millions of people to a better state.Ibrahim believes agriculture and education are areas where India can take the lead in AI development. She points to language as a moonshot. Think about India’s 100-plus languages, she says, and how long it took Google Translate to get there, and now AI can reach the dialects on top.Drug discovery is where the biggest claims for AI are being made and tested. Amodei’s blog might suggest that the next breakthrough cancer medicine is a prompt away.“That is not the case,” says David Ricks, chairman and CEO of Eli Lilly, in a conversation with Forbes India in early October. Medicines live in the physical world. Innovator companies make a molecule that does not exist—a new chemical structure to interfere with biology. And it must be safe. According to Ricks, there might only be a handful of medicines that can claim to be invented by AI and are in the human testing phase. However, making early-stage drug research more efficient is an efficient use case for AI.Drawing data from past laboratory experiments, Lilly’s models predict how a molecule might behave, how long it could remain active in the bloodstream, or whether it might cause unwanted effects. These predictions help scientists avoid spending time on candidates likely to fail, speeding up research and reducing costs.Arora says cost reduction is the secondary consideration; the solution and the speed of finding that solution are primary. “How much would you pay to cure cancer? Pick any number,” he says. “If I solve cancer, any form of cancer, does it matter how much it costs?”In drug discovery there are the so-called “orphan drugs”, which get abandoned because the market size is not big enough. Even though there might be 2,000 people in the world who have that disease, according to Arora, somebody decided that the amount of money required to solve that problem was not going to generate an adequate return. “Imagine, if you could solve every such case because of the availability of intelligence at the highest level on a cheap compute three to four years from now,” he says.India is the world’s third largest pharmaceutical producer by volume. Could AI help it move from being a hotbed of generics to becoming a land of innovators?“I think there is no reason why not,” says Arora.Also Read: Claude Cowork sparks SaaSpocalypse, Indian IT rewrites deal playbookGuardrails, not brakesWhile conversations around pacing AI development continue interspersed with calls for slowing it down, nobody is stopping the pace of research. All the frontier AI labs want to ensure that all the models released for public consumption have the right guardrails and testing in place.Arora points to a lunch at the White House, the seat of the US president, where the technology titans came up with a four-point plan: Audit internally, share the testing with a select group outside, take their input, and open the models to a third-party audit if required. A collective slowdown, he adds, is another matter.Ibrahim says humans have agency in shaping how AI is built and that the conversation on responsibility and safety across countries and communities is what is needed to ensure that humans remain in the lead. “We believe AI could be the most transformational technology of our time, and it requires exceptional care,” she says.For evidence, look no further than the use cases in India.| Photo by Aaron Schwartz / Bloomberg via Getty Images

After passing out of IIT-BHU, Varanasi, at the end of the 1980s, he went on to become Google’s chief business officer and its highest paid employee.
body: Later he was Soft.
Bank’s president and COO.
Currently, he is chairman and CEO of Palo Alto Networks—a position he has held since 2018.
By no account, though, has he ever been a farmer.
Yet, Arora is all agog when the subject of farming in India comes up, and quick to blend that with his career in technology.
Historically, he tells Forbes India in a video interview, a farmer besieged with questions will not have too many avenues to find the answers.
“I have put this particular seed in the ground.
It is the middle of summer, and I have been watering it, and nothing is happening.
What should I do?” Arora visualises a farmer wondering aloud.

“Historically,” he says, “that question went to a village elder or a panchayat meeting, and the answer depended on ‘wisdom, or tribal knowledge, embedded in somebody’s head who may have forgotten to take the weather into account.” Things have changed.
Now a farmer can photograph the soil and the field and put the question to an artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot.
In this way, Arora says, “We will be diffusing intelligence.” The diffusion, he believes, is the biggest thing AI is doing.
“If the internet democratised information, AI is going to democratise intelligence.” Arora is not the only one excited about how AI is transforming agriculture in India.

“It is a global challenge where India is absolutely leading,” says Lila Ibrahim, chief AI readiness officer at Google DeepMind, in an interview with Forbes India during her visit to New Delhi in the middle of October.
Brazilian farmers, as also those in a dozen other countries, are already learning from the way Indian farmers are using AI.
This would be music to the ears of those grappling with India’s growth conundrums.
Agriculture accounts for less than a fifth of the country’s gross domestic product (GDP) but employs about half its workforce.

Despite its importance to the country, agriculture has always been besieged with structural problems such as poor irrigation, fragmented holdings, poor connectivity with markets, soil degradation, poor crop planning, and susceptibility to climate change and weather shocks.
The mismatch between its share of GDP and of the workforce means it remains the key to removing the obstacles to inclusive growth.
The sector, says a Niti Aayog report published a year ago, “underpins employment generation, national health outcomes, and inclusive economic growth”.

More importantly, the paper says, “For India to achieve the status of a developed nation by 2047, its per capita Gross National Income must rise fivefold, a goal inseparable from achieving a commensurate increase in agrarian incomes and productivity.” This is what AI promises to change.
To be sure, agriculture is not the only sector in India where AI’s impact, going by the early signs, could turn things around.
There are already green shoots of transformation visible in education, health care, and others.
But let’s first get to agriculture.

Different language modelIndeed, farmers in India are speaking a different language, laced as it is with the latest information about changing weather patterns, crop planning, soil, nutrients and seeds.

A research paper published last year, the result of a collaboration between the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, the principal scientific advisor to the government of India, World Economic Forum, and BCG, identified 30 use cases for AI—spanning intelligent crop planning, smart farming and farm-to-fork solutions—in which AI can enhance productivity, sustainability and market connectivity.

In this mix you would also find Google DeepMind and Google Partner Innovation ploughing ahead with the technology giant’s initiative, AnthroKrishi, using AI and satellite imagery to create a farm-by-farm digital map of agriculture and helping farmers make better decisions based on real-time data.
AnthroKrishi is built to remove the barriers to using it, whether it is unlocking new markets or warning of a dry season.
However, this is not the first time technology is being used to sow fresh seeds of growth in agriculture.

Two-and-a-half decades ago, consumer goods giant ITC launched the e-Choupal initiative in Khasrod, Madhya Pradesh, to give rural farmers access to real-time weather, crop prices, and agricultural best practices via internet-connected computers in villages.
What is different this time?
The answer, says Ibrahim, lies in “real-time intelligence and the data patterns that I think we have never had access to before”.
Secondly, AI development is sprinting so fast that it makes the internet look like a marathon runner.
Four years ago, AI could barely write a line of code.
Today, as Anthropic’s Dario Amodei told the UN Security Council on September 23, it writes most of the code at his company and solves problems that have stumped mathematicians for decades.
The trajectory, he said, needs only a year or two more to reach what he calls a “country of geniuses in a data centre”.
That optimism has a dark side, too.
Earlier this year, an OpenAI agent breached open source platform Hugging Face’s systems and gained unauthorised access.
In September, the Australian government disclosed that an OpenAI agent had gained unauthorised access to non-public files on its Medicare health statistics portal.
Founders of frontier AI labs have warned about the pace at which AI is growing.
The risks they cite include the misuse of AI for cyberattacks, bioterrorism and economic disruption.
Former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon warned that AI could cause human extinction by 2030.

During the UN Security Council meeting, OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman said, “AI can either be more like a new Renaissance of creativity and discovery, or more like a new Industrial Revolution of upheaval and disarray.” Which is it going to be?
“Nobody talked about the negative narrative when airplanes were invented,” says Arora.

“This is the only technology where we seem to be talking about the dark side too soon.” India, however, is entering the conversation from an entirely different side, putting AI to work on its age-old problems of critical sectors such as education and health care, in addition, of course, to agriculture.
Beyond AnthroKrishi, Google DeepMind is working closely on gene mapping.
For instance, sorghum, also known as jowar, feeds half a billion people, yet its gene mapping is based largely on Western varieties, not the ones grown in India or Africa.

Google DeepMind partnered with ICRISAT, the international crops research institute headquartered in Hyderabad, to open a gene mapping catalogue for sorghum so that crop breeders can develop varieties that withstand heat and drought.
In education, the usual model is to have classrooms where a group of students is taught at the same time.
The knowledge passed on depends on the knowledge of the teacher.
You get a good teacher, you get interested in the subject, follow the teaching, and come out smart.
If not, the opposite becomes a possibility.
AI can tailor lessons to each child, go back over what a child has missed, and let them learn at their own pace.
“AI could be a teacher with immense patience, empathy, and can customise understanding or lack of knowledge accordingly,” says Arora.
In 2025, DeepMind worked to infuse Gemini (Google’s AI model) with its years of research on learning science.

In India, Ibrahim says, the Atal Tinkering Labs—school innovation labs run under the government’s Atal Innovation Mission—is an example of project-based learning with “a guide and a teacher at the centre of it”.
The partnership has helped DeepMind learn how India tests and teaches, she says, and could show what can be exported outside India.
“I think our education system is not necessarily designed to optimise for getting students in the workforce for the jobs that are available today, let alone in the future,” she says.
Then there is health care, where access remains a problem.
If someone in a remote village needs a doctor at one in the morning, they have no option but to get in the back of a truck and get driven to the nearest hospital just for an opinion.
That is about to change.

Non-profit organisations such as Wadhwani AI are deploying tools that enable frontline health workers to identify malnutrition in newborns, predict which pregnant women are at the risk of missing antenatal care, and more.

AI is also being embedded into government telemedicine platforms and, through assistants like HealthVaani, guiding ASHA (accredited social health activists) and other community health workers in local languages.
Similarly, startups such as qure.ai are using AI to analyse chest X-rays and CT scans, enabling faster detection of conditions such as tuberculosis and lung cancer.
This technology is useful in remote areas where radiologists are scarce.
Then there is manufacturing.

At Raychem RPG, the RPG Group’s energy solutions business, which makes accessories for joining high-voltage cables, the challenge is making sure work by employees and contract workers meets quality and safety standards at remote sites.

Workers photograph each stage of the job, and AI analyses the pictures to check that the right materials are in use and that conditions are safe, says Rajat Bhargava, CEO of the specialty sector and head of group transformation at RPG Group.

At CEAT, the tyre maker, visual analytics monitor the parameters that determine tyre quality, and AI helps flag quality issues and find ways to improve manufacturing yield, in several cases by double-digit percentages.
“Across around 130 major use cases at the group’s seven companies in the past year, the return has been about four times the investment,” says Bhargava.
Investors are looking for problems global AI is unlikely to prioritise, says Rishab Malik, partner at Jungle Ventures.
Companies that can solve local problems “faster, better, or in areas that larger LLMs will take time to get to, or will not find meaningful enough to solve”.
Between 50 and 60 percent of the early-stage deals Jungle sees involve AI in some form, he says.
One is Prosperr.io, an AI agent for filing taxes, a job many Indians hand to a chartered accountant for `5,000 to `6,000 each July.
It sends users 12 to 15 nudges through the year, with a human in the loop, and average revenue per user has gone as high as $80 to $90, Malik says.

He sees similar opportunities for an AI investment relationship manager for roughly 100 million Indians who earn in the `25 lakh to `5-6 crore bracket to manage their assets, as well as for an agentic wellness coach for the masses, priced at around `1000 per month.
Across all these, the idea is the same: Technology that meets people where they are.
“But it always takes a human in the lead.
It takes someone who knows what they really want to use the technology for,” says Ibrahim.

Malik says India has all the ingredients: “The risk appetite, the market access, the engineering talent, the capital.” Outside the US, India is the largest market in the world by usage, volume and queries.
Maybe not by monetisation yet, but it will get there, he says.
“It’s just a matter of time.
So, it’s not about if; it’s really about when.” Moonshot or mirage?
Globally, so far, the most prominent enterprise applications of AI have been in coding.
“There is no economic barrier to people in India being able to use coding models.
We are at no technological disadvantage.
People in India can use Claude Code as much as any country in the world,” says Arora.
India has the talent pool, and economic and technological parity to be able to make something out of it.
The focus, he says, should be on innovating in the application of AI, as opposed to the creation of models.
“Does it matter where the internet was born or who invented the mobile phone?
India has one of the most thriving populations leveraging the internet and the mobile phone in the cheapest possible way,” says Arora.
“It does not matter who builds the [AI] models.” The narrative should be about using them in the most efficient way as a nation to uplift millions of people to a better state.
Ibrahim believes agriculture and education are areas where India can take the lead in AI development.
She points to language as a moonshot.
Think about India’s 100-plus languages, she says, and how long it took Google Translate to get there, and now AI can reach the dialects on top.
Drug discovery is where the biggest claims for AI are being made and tested.
Amodei’s blog might suggest that the next breakthrough cancer medicine is a prompt away.
“That is not the case,” says David Ricks, chairman and CEO of Eli Lilly, in a conversation with Forbes India in early October.
Medicines live in the physical world.
Innovator companies make a molecule that does not exist—a new chemical structure to interfere with biology.
And it must be safe.
According to Ricks, there might only be a handful of medicines that can claim to be invented by AI and are in the human testing phase.
However, making early-stage drug research more efficient is an efficient use case for AI.
Drawing data from past laboratory experiments, Lilly’s models predict how a molecule might behave, how long it could remain active in the bloodstream, or whether it might cause unwanted effects.
These predictions help scientists avoid spending time on candidates likely to fail, speeding up research and reducing costs.
Arora says cost reduction is the secondary consideration; the solution and the speed of finding that solution are primary.
“How much would you pay to cure cancer?
Pick any number,” he says.
“If I solve cancer, any form of cancer, does it matter how much it costs?” In drug discovery there are the so-called “orphan drugs”, which get abandoned because the market size is not big enough.

Even though there might be 2,000 people in the world who have that disease, according to Arora, somebody decided that the amount of money required to solve that problem was not going to generate an adequate return.
“Imagine, if you could solve every such case because of the availability of intelligence at the highest level on a cheap compute three to four years from now,” he says.
India is the world’s third largest pharmaceutical producer by volume.
Could AI help it move from being a hotbed of generics to becoming a land of innovators?
“I think there is no reason why not,” says Arora.
Spocalypse, Indian.
IT rewrites deal playbookGuardrails, not brakes.
While conversations around pacing AI development continue interspersed with calls for slowing it down, nobody is stopping the pace of research.
All the frontier AI labs want to ensure that all the models released for public consumption have the right guardrails and testing in place.

Arora points to a lunch at the White House, the seat of the US president, where the technology titans came up with a four-point plan: Audit internally, share the testing with a select group outside, take their input, and open the models to a third-party audit if required.
A collective slowdown, he adds, is another matter.

Ibrahim says humans have agency in shaping how AI is built and that the conversation on responsibility and safety across countries and communities is what is needed to ensure that humans remain in the lead.
“We believe AI could be the most transformational technology of our time, and it requires exceptional care,” she says.

stories.title: Experts laud NPPA move on cancer drugs but bigger concerns remain
stories.summary: The Centre on October 17 notified that trade margins on 137 non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs would be capped at 30 percent of their maximum retail price (MRP) in a bid to make patients’ out-of-pocket costs more affordable. The measure, to be implemented from November 9, will cover branded and generic drugs, domestically manufactured and imported medicines, and patented and non-patented products. The government said that the reductions could lead to annual savings of Rs 2,500 crore.The move comes on the back of the Supreme Court questioning the government last week over rising costs and margins charged in the cancer treatment supply chain. Trade margin is the difference between the base price at which a manufacturer sells a drug to a distributor and the MRP paid by the patient.Also Read: Trump's tariffs: How exposed is Indian pharma?Parliamentary and public health committees report that roughly 70–80 percent of cancer costs are paid directly out of pocket. The drugs price regulator National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) found that the average trade mark-up on non-scheduled anti-cancer medicines was nearly 170 percent, with it reaching 700 percent in some instances. It invoked Paragraph 19 of the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013, which lets the government step in on prices in the public interest.The revised list, released on October 28, covers 543 brands and pack sizes, with cuts of up to 93 percent. Prices of drugs like RPG Life Sciences' Anastrozole fell from Rs 695.76 to Rs 73 for 10 tablets, and prices of biosimilar bevacizumab brand from Abbott fell from Rs 21,767.70 to Rs 5,930,13 for a 4 ml vial.Despite the move, doctors and analysts say the real test lies in seeing whether the lower prices actually reach patients, and whether it impacts the overall cost of cancer care, with some cautioning against assuming that whole classes of cancer treatment are now cheaper.A welcome step, with caveatsNirali Shah, research analyst at Ashika Investment Managers, said the move by the government is a game-changer for cancer-drug pricing in India, setting a stronger precedent for curbing excessive trade margins. “It puts pressure on brands that have relied on high mark-ups and favours companies with competitive pricing and efficient distribution," she says.Raziuddin Khwaja, a consultant in medical oncology at the Head and Neck Cancer Institute of India (HNCII), agrees on the positive impact of the price reduction but cautions against assuming that whole classes of treatment, (chemotherapy, immunotherapy, targeted and hormone therapy) are now cheaper. “Just because the price of some formulations has been reduced doesn't mean that the whole category has become more affordable. What a patient gains will depend on their cancer type, stage and prescribed regimen.” he says.Chemotherapy remains a cornerstone of cancer treatment, alongside surgery and radiotherapy. However, the therapeutic landscape is rapidly expanding with the integration of immunotherapy, targeted therapy and hormonal treatment.Khwaja says that immunotherapy, in particular, is one of the most rapidly advancing fields in oncology. “The growing impact of immunotherapy is reflected in a 2025 study by Warwar et al., published in the Journal of Surgical Oncology. Analysing 1,425,731 patients with Stage IV cancers from the US National Cancer Database, the study reported an increase in immunotherapy utilisation from 1 percent in 2004–2010 to 24.6 percent in 2016–2020,” he said.While prices of some brands dropped, several originator brands have not changed the prices. Roche's Avastin stayed at Rs 1.23 lakh per 400 mg vial, MSD's immunotherapy Keytruda at Rs 2.16 lakh, and prices of nivolumab brands were unchanged. Officials said cuts applied only where high MRPs came from large trade margins. Since the list relies on data from the company, the regulator said it will update it periodically.Sachin Almel, section head of medical oncology at PD Hinduja Hospital and Medical Research Centre in Mumbai, describes it as an essential step for a low- and middle-income country like India, calling for the list to be widened. “Most of the drugs covered are chemotherapy agents, and rituximab, used in some blood cancers, is the only immunotherapy on it. There needs to be expansion of the current list to include more immunotherapy drugs also,” he says.Also Read: Appetite for Ozempic wanesDisproportionate savingsExperts are of the opinion that a lower drug price does not mean an equally lower treatment bill. Almel says that patients also pay for investigations, surgery, radiation, hospital stays, follow-ups and managing side effects. "Only reduction in drug prices won't help much,” he adds.Khwaja notes that the relief could be substantial for patients who pay for costly medicines themselves over many months, but will vary for those covered by insurance or patient assistance programmes (PAPs). "It would be of little use to announce a reduction in price if patients don't experience the benefit when buying their medication," he says. The aim, he adds, should be to ensure that money worries do not make patients delay, stop or cut back on recommended treatment.PAPs are manufacturer-funded programmes offering free or discounted medicines to eligible patients. PAPs can reduce expenses by up to 60 percent for immunotherapy and targeted therapy. Almel says PAPs offer eligible patients free or discounted medicines, but benefits vary, and their exclusion “raises concerns about transparency and the true extent of savings”.Khwaja points out that PAPs often come with eligibility criteria and paperwork, and not everyone who needs help can access them. He adds: “These programmes are intended to help with affordability, not to replace it.”Access and affordability remain the bigger problemAmidst all these concerns, the core issue in Indian cancer care is the affordability of the best available treatment. For most patients, insurance coverage varies by policy, treatment type and sum insured, and majority of patients have a very limited coverage.Khwaja adds that many patients reach hospitals only once the disease is advanced, which makes treatment harder, longer and costlier. He says that there is low awareness, delay in seeking care, limited diagnostics, and a wide gap in access between big cities and smaller towns. Even insured families may face co-payments, exclusions and limits, as well as travel and accommodation costs, and lost income.Patented therapies pose another problem. Drug prices reflect research and development costs, patents, and limited competition, and can be regulated only when there is healthy competition and there are available biosimilars with strict price regulation. Khwaja notes that India's market is not entirely unregulated, but there is no uniform price cap on innovator and foreign-branded cancer drugs, which keeps several of them out of reach.“The larger challenge remains the high cost of patented therapies and inadequate insurance coverage,” Shah says. “This is a significant step towards making cancer medicines more affordable. The next priority is ensuring that lower prices translate into sustained access to treatment.”

The move comes on the back of the Supreme Court questioning the government last week over rising costs and margins charged in the cancer treatment supply chain.

It invoked Paragraph 19 of the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013, which lets the government step in on prices in the public interest.

Despite the move, doctors and analysts say the real test lies in seeing whether the lower prices actually reach patients, and whether it impacts the overall cost of cancer care, with some cautioning against assuming that whole classes of cancer treatment are now cheaper.

A welcome step, with caveatsNirali Shah, research analyst at Ashika Investment Managers, said the move by the government is a game-changer for cancer-drug pricing in India, setting a stronger precedent for curbing excessive trade margins.
“It puts pressure on brands that have relied on high mark-ups and favours companies with competitive pricing and efficient distribution," she says.

Raziuddin Khwaja, a consultant in medical oncology at the Head and Neck Cancer Institute of India (HNCII), agrees on the positive impact of the price reduction but cautions against assuming that whole classes of treatment, (chemotherapy, immunotherapy, targeted and hormone therapy) are now cheaper.
“Just because the price of some formulations has been reduced doesn't mean that the whole category has become more affordable.
What a patient gains will depend on their cancer type, stage and prescribed regimen.” he says.
Chemotherapy remains a cornerstone of cancer treatment, alongside surgery and radiotherapy.
However, the therapeutic landscape is rapidly expanding with the integration of immunotherapy, targeted therapy and hormonal treatment.
Khwaja says that immunotherapy, in particular, is one of the most rapidly advancing fields in oncology.
“The growing impact of immunotherapy is reflected in a 2025 study by Warwar et al., published in the Journal of Surgical Oncology.
While prices of some brands dropped, several originator brands have not changed the prices.
Roche's Avastin stayed at Rs 1.23 lakh per 400 mg vial, MSD's immunotherapy Keytruda at Rs 2.16 lakh, and prices of nivolumab brands were unchanged.
Since the list relies on data from the company, the regulator said it will update it periodically.

Sachin Almel, section head of medical oncology at PD Hinduja Hospital and Medical Research Centre in Mumbai, describes it as an essential step for a low- and middle-income country like India, calling for the list to be widened.
“Most of the drugs covered are chemotherapy agents, and rituximab, used in some blood cancers, is the only immunotherapy on it.
There needs to be expansion of the current list to include more immunotherapy drugs also,” he says.
Disproportionate savingsExperts are of the opinion that a lower drug price does not mean an equally lower treatment bill.
Almel says that patients also pay for investigations, surgery, radiation, hospital stays, follow-ups and managing side effects.
"Only reduction in drug prices won't help much,” he adds.

Khwaja notes that the relief could be substantial for patients who pay for costly medicines themselves over many months, but will vary for those covered by insurance or patient assistance programmes (PAPs).
"It would be of little use to announce a reduction in price if patients don't experience the benefit when buying their medication," he says.
The aim, he adds, should be to ensure that money worries do not make patients delay, stop or cut back on recommended treatment.
PAPs are manufacturer-funded programmes offering free or discounted medicines to eligible patients.
PAPs can reduce expenses by up to 60 percent for immunotherapy and targeted therapy.
Almel says PAPs offer eligible patients free or discounted medicines, but benefits vary, and their exclusion “raises concerns about transparency and the true extent of savings”.
Khwaja points out that PAPs often come with eligibility criteria and paperwork, and not everyone who needs help can access them.

He adds: “These programmes are intended to help with affordability, not to replace it.” Access and affordability remain the bigger problemAmidst all these concerns, the core issue in Indian cancer care is the affordability of the best available treatment.
For most patients, insurance coverage varies by policy, treatment type and sum insured, and majority of patients have a very limited coverage.
Khwaja adds that many patients reach hospitals only once the disease is advanced, which makes treatment harder, longer and costlier.
He says that there is low awareness, delay in seeking care, limited diagnostics, and a wide gap in access between big cities and smaller towns.
Even insured families may face co-payments, exclusions and limits, as well as travel and accommodation costs, and lost income.
Patented therapies pose another problem.

Drug prices reflect research and development costs, patents, and limited competition, and can be regulated only when there is healthy competition and there are available biosimilars with strict price regulation.
Khwaja notes that India's market is not entirely unregulated, but there is no uniform price cap on innovator and foreign-branded cancer drugs, which keeps several of them out of reach.
“The larger challenge remains the high cost of patented therapies and inadequate insurance coverage,” Shah says.
“This is a significant step towards making cancer medicines more affordable.
The next priority is ensuring that lower prices translate into sustained access to treatment.”

article_sentences: The police cited security and traffic concerns to justify the de-notification of Jantar Mantar as a protest site.
The Delhi Police Commissioner has filed an affidavit before the Supreme Court defending the de-notification of Jantar Mantar as a designated protest site.
He states that the decision was taken keeping in mind public interest and as per the Supreme Court's observation, no one can claim an absolute right to protest at a particular location.

The Delhi Police Commissioner states that following de-notification of Jantar Mantar as a designated protest site, 3 alternate sites have been designated/redesignated for holding protests/demonstrations - Ramlila Maidan (Central Delhi), CBD Ground (East Delhi) and Burari Ground (North West Delhi).
"It may be pointed out at the outset that Jantar Mantar is not a 'site' as understood but is, in fact, a public road.

Being a public road, it ought not to have been declared as a designated protest site since it continues to be used [though with difficulty] as a public road," Commissioner Anurag Kumar stated in response to the writ petition filed by Swaty Singh.
As per the affidavit, with the advent of technology and social media, the proximity of a protest site to the seat of the government has "ceased to be relevant and has become redundant".
The affidavit states that the decision to de-notify Jantar Mantar as a protest site was taken by the Delhi.

Police Commissioner "after due consideration of the relevant factors and criteria" and upon consideration of the recommendations of the Committee constituted by the Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India.
It is said that the decision was taken in the interest of maintaining public order and larger public interest.

The Delhi Police Commissioner has categorically denied as "incorrect" the claim that Jantar Mantar was de-notified as designated protest site pursuant to the Court's order dated October 9 (whereby authorities were issued notice on the plea challenging de-notification of Jantar Mantar as a designated protest site and asked to consider alternate sites).

"It is submitted that the proposed change in the notified venue for protests had been under consideration of the deponent and the Central Government for a considerable period in view of the changed circumstances".

stories.headline: NC hits back at Aga Ruhullah, terms his speech ‘manifestation of mental, moral bankruptcy’
stories.title: NC hits back at Aga Ruhullah, terms his speech ‘manifestation of mental, moral bankruptcy’
stories.summary: Srinagar, Nov 3: Jammu and Kashmir National Conference (JKNC) on Tuesday termed Aga Syed Ruhullah Mehdi's speech as a manifestation of his “mental and moral bankruptcy” and an example of his “self-obsession”.NC hits back at Aga Ruhullah, terms his speech ‘manifestation of mental, moral bankruptcy’ In a post on X, JKNC said while invoking the holy Quran and the divine message of dignity and respect for human beings, Ruhullah's speech was full of derogatory, abusive and unparliamentary language against NC leadership. "The language used by him only reflects who he is," the party said. "Since Aga Ruhullah has chosen to use the issue of special status and reservation to resign from NC, it's important to keep the record straight. He only remembered to resign when he was told to by the party president. The same way he only remembered 2010 today when it suited him. He is a man who happily remained in office as a minister in 2010 until he was removed in a general reshuffle. He was happy to fight elections in 2014 on JKNC ticket and didn't remember 2010 then. In fact he conveniently forgot all about it until 2026, 16 years later," NC said. The party asked whether Ruhullah was not the first to welcome the resolution demanding restoration of special status, passed by the J&K Assembly on November 6. Didn't he say that it was the promise that had been delivered? "What has Aga Ruhullah done in Parliament on special status. Wasn't he elected to the parliament to represent the sentiment of people and garner support of secular parties and MPs in the parliament. Aga Ruhullah Mehdi was able to gather signatures of over 100 MPs from different parties in the parliament to move an impeachment motion against Allahabad High Court judge Shekar Kumar Yadav. Can he tell us if he ever made such an effort to gather signatures of MPs for the restoration of special status or statehood? Did he even try to move a resolution or bill in the parliament in this regard?" NC asked. The party said Ruhullah was sent to parliament to speak about the dispossession and how people's will represented by the elected government has been undermined and belittled by the central government and its appointed Lt Governor in an attempt to delegitimise the vote and elected government. "Did he speak even once - that even under the current UT arrangement, the departments which are technically under elected government are not allowed to function and LG continues to run them through remote control?" NC asked. The party said Ruhullah started his opposition to elected government on the issue of reservation in jobs, a grave injustice to the open merit category. "It's indeed a grave injustice committed during LGs rule. NC raised this issue made it an important part of its election manifesto and promised to change it. Ironically, Aga and his ilk chose to blame the whistleblower for the problem. Did he ever utter a single word against LG and central government for snatching jobs of open merit category?" the party said. "In accordance with its election promise, NC government formed a cabinet sub-committee and made first significant changes in the reservations. The file has been stalled by the powers that be. Did Mr Mehdi, raise this issue in the parliament and ask the centre why they have stalled the J&K cabinet decision on Reservation in jobs? Aga sb was elected as MP six months before Assembly elections and formation of elected government in J&K. Did he organise a single protest against the LG and demanded justice for open merit? Did he raise the issue of multiple fraud recruitments and exams and how job aspirants of one region were systematically removed from the system and jobs?" NC said. The party said while the NC government knows its limitations given the present scheme of things, it has carefully chosen its roadmap on the issues which are directly linked to existence and identity. "Our thrust on restoration of statehood is not and will never be at the expense of the special status. If it was so, the first transaction of business of this government would not have been the special status. And August 15 of CM would not have reiterated it. Protection and preservation of our identity and constitutional rights form the foundation of NCs political ideology. Abandoning it means abandoning the party and the politics it has stood for last over 90 years. Reclaiming and repossessing what was taken away from us needs a deft politics, not theatrics. Theatrics will not take us anywhere. It may temporarily grab some attention and social media likes, but in the long run it will not achieve anything for people," NC said. The party said Aga Ruhullah's decision to resign as MP is too late. "He should have done a year ago when he chose to join the forces who were rattled by the mandate to NC. While sitting in NC, he became instrumental in the defeat of the party in the assembly by-elections of the Budgam seat. Where was his conscience then? Backstabbing the same party he owed his political existence. Isn't it astonishing that someone who owes his whole political existence to NC, started his politics in the party, remained MLA for three terms, minister in the government and MP of the party is so brazenly showing his narcissistic conduct and finding all faults in the party after 25 years," NC added.
